Argentines stretched for miles down the Avenida del Libertador, waving the white-and-yellow Vatican flag and pressing against security barriers for a glimpse of the pontiff at the largest event yet of the pope’s 12-day South American tour, and of his 18-month tenure leading the global Catholic Church.
Chants of “Long live Pope Leo!” echoed down the tree-lined street as the ​pope was driven by in an open-top popemobile under sunny skies.
Pope Leo XIV and Argentina’s President Javier Milei take part in a welcome ceremony at Jorge Newbery International airport in Buenos Aires on November 8 [AFP]
Leo said in his sermon how happy he was to see Catholics in a region that ​has long been a stronghold for the Church but where it has been losing ground recently to fast-growing evangelical denominations.
“It fills my heart ⁠with joy to celebrate… with you,” said the pope. “My visit to this land of Argentina has allowed me to see on your faces the enthusiasm of your faith.”
Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 50-event, three-country tour less than a month after undergoing lung cancer surgery. He visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday and ​will travel on to Peru on Wednesday before returning to Rome on November 17.
The first US-born pope spent decades as a missionary in Peru and the Vatican has described the tour, one of the most demanding foreign tours by a pope in decades, as a “homecoming”.
People had gathered in the early hours of Monday ahead of the Mass. Some normally bustling parts of the city stood near-empty as police cordoned ​off a security zone.
Vendors along the pilgrims’ route were selling souvenirs of the visit, including flags featuring the pope’s face.
“I love that (Leo) is visiting us,” said Claudia Pardo, 37, ​who waited for Leo with her husband and two young children. “It’s a unique, historic moment, and we should listen to his message.”
Alejandra Frias, 56, was sleepless after camping out all night to get a front-row ‌view of the pope. “This ⁠is an emotional and spiritual moment,” she said.
A pope has not visited majority-Catholic Argentina since 1987.
Leo has emerged as a forceful voice on the world stage, lamenting what he sees as a failure of global leadership. On his tour he has urged South American nations to set an example of regional cooperation and patient diplomacy instead of conflict.
On Sunday, the pope addressed Argentine President Javier Milei, a libertarian seen as a close ally of US President Donald Trump. He urged Milei, who has pushed an austerity agenda ​that the Church has strongly criticized for ​cutting social services, to not target Argentina’s poorest.
He ⁠also told Milei, a theatrical figure known for bombastic statements, that leaders should be careful with their words and know the limits of their power.
The pope lamented the difficulties faced by Argentine families at the Mass on Monday. He said they are enduring “instability, social ​hardship, precarious employment, domestic violence, painful separations and addictions that destroy young people’s futures and damage family relationships.”
Ahead of Monday’s ⁠Mass, Leo visited a care center for people with disabilities on the southern outskirts of Buenos Aires, where thousands had also gathered in hope of seeing him.
Jorge Silanes, religious director of the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione center that welcomed Leo, said the visit carried added significance because Milei’s spending cuts have reduced disability benefits while poverty remains widespread.
Leo said in remarks that centers ⁠like theirs “have much ​to say to our societies, which are often driven solely by the pursuit of economic success.”
“A nation’s ​progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs,” said the pope.
The previous largest event in Leo’s papacy came in June, when some 1.2 million turned out in Madrid during the pontiff’s ​visit to Spain.
